title: NGC 1003
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1003, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1003 stands out in this deep view, while behind it lie small red galaxies belonging to a more distant cluster. It comes from a 70-minute observation with the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, which is located at Kitt Peak National Observatory, part of NSF NOIRLab.

NGC 1003, in the direction of Perseus, sits in front of that galaxy cluster, a vast gathering of galaxies held together by their gravity. Background galaxies like these are usually overlooked because they are so faint, but this long exposure collected enough light to capture them.

A long exposure works by letting light build up on the camera for far longer than the eye can gather it, so faint objects slowly accumulate enough signal to appear. Very distant galaxies can also look redder than nearby ones, partly because the expansion of the Universe stretches their light toward longer wavelengths during its journey.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic I camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through U, B, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
